title: Long sentences that still make sense
goal: Build long formal sentences that hold together: subordinate clauses with the right connector and comma, opening phrases such as *Setelah membaca…* and *Dengan mempertimbangkan…*, and none of the English calques (*di mana*, *yang mana*, *dari satu sama lain*) that give translated Indonesian away.
bekal: replace relative *di mana* and *yang mana* with *tempat*, *ketika* or plain *yang*
open a sentence with *Setelah…*, *Dengan mempertimbangkan…* or *Berdasarkan…* and keep the right subject after the comma
translate meaning rather than words: *saling belajar*, *program yang didanai kedua negara*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Ringkasan kebijakan
dialogs.intro: Monday, 5 March 2029. The meeting with Ibu Maria went well, and she has asked for a two-page policy brief. Sarah is writing it with Dr. Lestari Wibowo, her partner from the Sumberwangi project, who moved from UGM to a university in Jakarta last year.

lines.speaker: Lestari:
lines.text: Sarah, kalimat pembukamu sudah bagus, tapi ada ‘di mana’ yang salah tempat.
lines.id: Sarah, your opening sentence is good, but there's a ‘di mana’ in the wrong place.
lines.literal: Sarah, sentence opening-your already good, but exist ‘at where’ that wrong place.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Yang mana, Bu? ‘Sekolah di mana guru-guru kami mengajar’?

lines.text: Ya. ‘Di mana’ itu kata tanya. Tulis saja ‘sekolah tempat guru-guru kami mengajar’.
lines.id: Yes. ‘Di mana’ is a question word. Just write ‘sekolah tempat guru-guru kami mengajar’.
lines.literal: yes. ‘at where’ that word ask. write just ‘school place teacher-teacher our teach’.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Oh, begitu. Itu terjemahan langsung dari ‘where’, ya.
lines.id: I see. That's a straight translation of ‘where’.
lines.literal: oh, like-that. that translation direct from ‘where’, [ya].

lines.speaker: Lestari:
lines.text: Persis. Sama dengan ‘yang mana’ untuk ‘which’. Cukup ‘yang’.
lines.id: Exactly. The same goes for ‘yang mana’ for ‘which’. Plain ‘yang’ is enough.
lines.literal: exact. same with ‘that which’ for ‘which’. enough ‘that’.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Paragraf kedua bagaimana? Menurut saya terlalu banyak ‘dan’.
lines.id: What about the second paragraph? I think there are too many ‘and’s.
lines.literal: paragraph second how? according-to me too many ‘and’.

lines.speaker: Lestari:
lines.text: Coba dipecah. Mulai dengan ‘Setelah mengikuti program ini, …’.
lines.id: Try splitting it up. Start with ‘After taking part in this programme, …’.
lines.literal: try be-split. start with ‘after follow programme this, …’.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: ‘… guru peserta mampu menerapkan metode baru di kelas.’ Begitu?
lines.id: ‘… participating teachers are able to apply new methods in class.’ Like that?
lines.literal: ‘… teacher participant able apply method new at class.’ like-that?

lines.speaker: Lestari:
lines.text: Ya, dan subjeknya harus sama. Yang mengikuti program itu gurunya, bukan metodenya.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Lalu rekomendasinya saya awali dengan ‘Dengan mempertimbangkan hasil survei, …’?

lines.speaker: Lestari:
lines.text: Bagus. Sesudah koma langsung subjeknya: ‘kami merekomendasikan agar …’.
lines.id: Good. After the comma, go straight to the subject: ‘we recommend that …’.
lines.literal: good. after comma directly subject-the: ‘we recommend so-that …’.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: ‘… kementerian memperluas program ini ke lima provinsi.’ Tidak terlalu berani?
lines.id: ‘… the ministry extend the programme to five provinces.’ Isn't that too bold?
lines.literal: ‘… ministry widen programme this to five province.’ not too brave?

lines.speaker: Lestari:
lines.text: Ringkasan kebijakan memang harus berani, asalkan datanya kuat.
lines.id: A policy brief is supposed to be bold, as long as the data is solid.
lines.literal: summary policy indeed must brave, provided data-the strong.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Datanya kuat, Bu. Tiga ratus guru, dua belas sekolah, dua negara.
lines.id: The data's solid. Three hundred teachers, twelve schools, two countries.
lines.literal: data-the strong, Mrs. three hundred teacher, two teen school, two country.

lines.speaker: Lestari:
lines.text: Kalau begitu, kalimat itu tidak perlu diubah satu huruf pun.
lines.id: In that case, that sentence doesn't need a single letter changed.
lines.literal: if like-that, sentence that not need be-changed one letter [pun].

notes: **Di mana is a question.** *Di mana kantornya?* is perfect Indonesian. Using it to join two clauses, as English does with “where”, is a calque from English (and from Dutch before it), and editors strike it out. For places, use *tempat*: *sekolah tempat guru kami mengajar*.

**Yang mana** has the same problem. As a question it is fine (*Yang mana, Bu?* — “Which one?”, as Sarah herself says a line later). As a relative pronoun copying “which”, it is redundant: plain *yang* already does the job.

**Coba dipecah** — “try splitting it”. *Coba* + passive verb is a very common polite instruction among colleagues: *coba dicek*, *coba dibaca lagi*. It sounds gentler than an imperative because nobody is named as the one who must do it.

**Setelah mengikuti program ini, …** has no subject of its own: it borrows the subject of the main clause. So the main clause must begin with whoever did the “following” (*guru peserta*), which is exactly Dr. Lestari's point. More on this in the second grammar box.

**Merekomendasikan agar** — “to recommend that”. After *agar* comes a full clause with its own subject and an active verb: *agar kementerian memperluas program*. Indonesian has no subjunctive, so the verb does not change.
**Satu huruf pun** — “not even one letter”. *Pun* after a word in a negative sentence means “even”: *satu rupiah pun*, *sedikit pun*. As Unit 1 showed, it is written as a separate word here.

grammars.title: Where, which, in which: the calque trap
body: English relative words tempt learners, and plenty of Indonesian writers, into literal copies. Standard Indonesian has *yang* for almost everything, *tempat* for places and *ketika* or *saat* for times.

head: Calque (avoid)
Standard
English
rows: the schools where our teachers teach
the house where I was born
the year in which the programme began
the report which has been sent
the teacher with whom I work

after: The last row is the hardest habit to break. English likes to hang a “which” on the end of a sentence to comment on the whole thing. Indonesian starts a new sentence with *Hal ini* or *Hal itu*: *Datanya kuat. Hal ini membuat rekomendasi kami meyakinkan.*
In speech you will hear *di mana* and *yang mana* used as relatives all the time, on television, in lectures and in parliament. That is exactly why the UKBI and every editor test it.

grammars.title: Opening phrases that borrow their subject
body: Formal Indonesian often opens with a verb phrase that has no subject of its own. It borrows the subject of the main clause, so that subject must be the one who does the action.

head: Opener
English
Example
rows: *Setelah membaca laporan itu, Ibu Maria menelepon kami.*
*Untuk mencapai target itu, sekolah perlu dua guru tambahan.*
*Berdasarkan data tahun lalu, jumlah peserta naik.*

after: ⚠️ The dangling opener: *Setelah membaca laporan itu, rapat dimulai* says that the meeting read the report. Put the reader in the subject slot: *Setelah membaca laporan itu, kami memulai rapat.*
*Berdasarkan* is the one exception: it takes a noun, not an action, so it does not need a matching subject. And whenever an opener comes first, EYD wants a comma after it.

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Terjemahan Yoga
dialogs.intro: Thursday, 15 March. The Australian partner has sent a one-page summary in English for the brief's appendix. Yoga translated it overnight. Sarah reads it at her desk while he waits.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Yoga, terjemahanmu cepat sekali. Tapi coba baca kalimat ini.
lines.id: Yoga, that was a very fast translation. But read this sentence.
lines.literal: Yoga, translation-your fast very. but try read sentence this.

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: ‘Program ini adalah program di mana guru-guru bisa belajar dari satu sama lain.’ Kenapa, Mbak?
lines.id: ‘This programme is a programme where teachers can learn from one another.’ What's wrong with it?
lines.literal: ‘programme this is programme at where teacher-teacher can learn from one same other.’ why, Miss?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Dua masalah: ‘di mana’ dan ‘dari satu sama lain’. Dua-duanya bahasa Inggris.
lines.id: Two problems: ‘di mana’ and ‘dari satu sama lain’. They're both English.
lines.literal: two problem: ‘at where’ and ‘from one same other’. two-both language English.

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Waduh. Jadi harusnya ‘Dalam program ini, guru-guru saling belajar’?
lines.id: Oh dear. So it should be ‘In this programme, teachers learn from each other’?
lines.literal: oh-dear. so should-be ‘in programme this, teacher-teacher mutually learn’?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Nah, itu. ‘Saling’ sudah cukup. Kalimat berikutnya?
lines.id: That's it. ‘Saling’ is enough. Next sentence?
lines.literal: [nah], that. ‘mutually’ already enough. sentence next?

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: ‘Dengan dukungan kedua pemerintah, program ini akan diperluas.’ Ini aman, kan?
lines.id: ‘With the support of both governments, the programme will be expanded.’ This one's fine, isn't it?
lines.literal: ‘with support both government, programme this will be-widened.’ this safe, [kan]?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Aman. Tapi ‘Being funded by…’ di paragraf tiga kamu terjemahkan ‘Menjadi didanai oleh…’.
lines.id: Fine. But in paragraph three you translated ‘Being funded by…’ as ‘Menjadi didanai oleh…’.
lines.literal: safe. but ‘being funded by…’ at paragraph three you translate ‘become be-funded by…’.

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Hehe, itu jam dua pagi, Mbak. Mungkin ‘Karena didanai oleh…’?
lines.id: Heh, that was two in the morning. Maybe ‘Karena didanai oleh…’?
lines.literal: hehe, that hour two morning, Miss. maybe ‘because be-funded by…’?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Bisa. Atau lebih ringkas: ‘Program yang didanai kedua negara ini …’. Jangan terjemahkan kata per kata.
lines.id: That works. Or more concisely: ‘This programme, funded by both countries, …’. Don't translate word for word.
lines.literal: can. or more concise: ‘programme that be-funded both country this …’. don't translate word per word.

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Siap. Terjemahkan maknanya, bukan kata-katanya. Aku catat, Mbak.
lines.id: Got it. Translate the meaning, not the words. I'm writing that down.
lines.literal: ready. translate meaning-its, not word-word-its. I note, Miss.

notes: **Dari satu sama lain** copies “from one another”. Indonesian shows that an action goes both ways with *saling* in front of the verb: *saling belajar*, *saling membantu*, *saling menghormati*. *Satu sama lain* exists, but it goes after the verb (*belajar satu sama lain*), never after *dari*.

**Waduh** is the all-purpose “oh dear, oops”, Javanese in origin and heard all over Java. *Harusnya* is the everyday *seharusnya*, “it should be”. Yoga's *aku* with his boss is typical of young Jakarta offices where the boss is only a few years older.

**Menjadi + passive** is Yoga's 2 a.m. rendering of the English “being”. *Menjadi* means “to become” and cannot carry a passive. Indonesian has no participles, so the English “-ing” and “-ed” phrases are rebuilt with *karena*, *setelah*, or a *yang* clause.

**Kedua pemerintah** — “both governments”. Before a noun, *kedua* means “both” (*kedua negara*, *kedua tangan*); after a noun, it means “second” (*pemerintah kedua*, *paragraf kedua*). The same word, and its position decides.

**Didanai** — “funded”, from *dana* (funds) with *di-…-i*. The family: *mendanai* (to fund), *pendanaan* (funding), *dana hibah* (grant money). *Diperluas* is from *luas* (wide) with *memper-*: to widen, expand.

**Makna vs arti.** Both mean “meaning”. *Arti* is the everyday word (*Apa artinya?*); *makna* is more formal and suggests deeper sense or significance (*makna sebuah kata*, *makna Lebaran*). Sarah's maxim uses *makna* because translation is exactly about that deeper sense.

grammars.title: English skeletons, Indonesian skin
body: Yoga's mistakes are the ones every translator makes at 2 a.m.: the English structure shows through the Indonesian words. Here are the most common skeletons and what Indonesian does instead.
after: The cure is always the same: read the English, close it, and write what it means the way an Indonesian would say it. If the result is shorter, it is probably better.

*Adalah* deserves a special warning. English needs “is” in every sentence; Indonesian uses *adalah* only to link two nouns (*Jakarta adalah ibu kota*) and drops it before adjectives: *Ini penting*, never *Ini adalah penting*.

blocks.text: A complex sentence is a main clause plus one or more subordinate clauses, each introduced by a connector. These are the connectors a formal text lives on.

The comma rule: when the subordinate clause comes first, put a comma after it (*Karena hujan, rapat ditunda*). When the main clause comes first, no comma (*Rapat ditunda karena hujan*). Remember from Unit 2: one connector per link, so never *karena … maka* or *meskipun … tetapi*.
A *ringkasan kebijakan* (policy brief) is short, argued and written for a busy official. Its parts and their typical opening sentences:

blocks.title: Sarah's recommendation, final version
items: Setelah mengikuti program ini, guru peserta mampu menerapkan metode baru di kelas.
Dengan mempertimbangkan hasil survei terhadap tiga ratus guru di dua belas sekolah, kami merekomendasikan agar kementerian memperluas program ini ke lima provinsi.
